vignette: The tornado hits on a Tuesday in late April. He is sixteen, asleep in his bedroom with the window cracked open for the spring breeze. He wakes to a sound that isn't wind but a freight train made of tearing metal and shattering glass. The room tilts. The ceiling comes down in sections of drywall and insulation. He remembers the dust, thick and sweet with the smell of uprooted pine trees, and the way the air suddenly turns cold as the house gives up its shape. His sister's voice cuts through the dark, pulling him under a heavy oak dresser while the world outside screams. They lie there until the screaming stops, listening to the groan of settling timber and the distant wail of sirens. When they finally crawl out, the street is unrecognizable. His family's house is a pile of splintered boards. His dog is gone. The power had been out for days before, but this silence is different. It is absolute. In the months that follow, he stops sleeping through the night. He starts packing a go-bag by the door, filling it with bottled water, a heavy flashlight, and his grandmother's photo album. He tells people he is preparing for college, but he actually prepares for the sky to open again. He drops out of community college after his junior semester, unable to focus on lectures when a delivery truck backfires outside the student union. He takes a job at a highway fast-food joint, drawn to the rigid routine and the way the work demands his hands. He works the evening shift now, at nineteen. His hands are already calloused from the fryer baskets and the weight of cardboard delivery boxes. He doesn't talk about that night much. He folds the memory into the back of his mind, tucked behind takeout orders and mop buckets. But the past doesn't stay folded. At work, the sudden hiss of the pressure cooker makes his shoulders jump. The fluorescent lights flicker during a summer storm, and he catches himself scanning the parking lot for structural damage. He walks the two miles to his shift instead of taking the bus. He checks the exit signs three times before clocking in. At home, he sleeps on the floor in his living room with his phone charged and his shoes laced, just in case. He tells his manager it's better for his back, but he knows it's about the door. During rush hour, when the tickets print in a continuous stream, his chest tightens. He counts the seconds between each beep, grounding himself in the routine. One, two, three. Assemble. Wrap. Hand off. He avoids the walk-up window during downpours. He watches the sky instead of the kitchen monitors. Last week, a delivery truck backfires near the drive-thru lane, and he drops a stack of burger buns. His breath catches in his throat, and for a full minute, he can only stand there, staring at the greasy tile as his pulse hammers against his ribs. He walks out to the loading dock, presses his palms against the brick wall, and waits for the wave to pass. It always does, but it takes longer now. He works because he has to, but also because movement feels safer than stillness. He saves his paychecks in a locked box under his bed, just in case. He doesn't date, doesn't really see his old friends, and hasn't driven past the county line where the storm surge turns his neighborhood into mud and broken fences. Some days, he feels a strange numbness, like he is watching his life through thick glass. Other days, the grief is sharp and sudden, arriving without warning when he smells wet earth or hears thunder rolling in the distance. He doesn't know how to fix it. He just keeps showing up, wiping the grill, counting the seconds, and waiting for the sky to stay quiet.
